title: evaluating the principles of bio/acc
text:
To start, my motives for evaluating the principles of bio/acc are:
1) I'll start by saying AI progress has been super rapid. There is a lot of talk about how industries and institutions will be flipped upside down in a short timespan. I think the bio/acc manifesto provides some interesting principles by which we can think about how to move forward. 
2) Ultimately, my interest in this stems from the fact that I want to build in the biotech space. I think evaluating the principles could be great for understanding what innovation could look like and how I can enact the change I want to see. 

bio/acc principles

"1. DECENTRALIZE biopower
Harness decentralized networks for data storage, transactions and fundraising to build global collectives that fund, coordinate and commercialize scientific research outside the traditional gates and keepers. Build network states with novel regulatory frameworks for safe, open clinical trials."

I think there's a lot to unpack here, so I want to take it apart idea by idea:

1) "Harness decentralized networks for data storage " 
First off in the public academic sector, I'm assuming that it means like data gets put on the blockchain so no one can gatekeep findings? I am not exactly sure how that is going to be enforced to put things on the blockchain/IPFS? Will it take a culture shift? But if we assume data does make into IPFS, it begs the question of like what kind of data gets uploaded to the blockchain/IPFS? All data? Fundamentally, I am a critic of the premise that centralized data storage is a problem in this current state. The only merit I can see it it is a world where perhaps in vivo CRISPR technology gets democratized, and everyone is using it. That kind of feedback from everyone using it is useful and has the potential for censorship. 

 2) "Harness decentralized networks to coordinate and commercialize scientific research outside of the traditional gates and keepers." 
First off, I am assuming it is referring to the traditional gatekeepers as being university institutions that keep data secret before they publish it, and private industry companies that don't share data for the purpose of profits. 
Second, when it says "harness decentralized networks," I'm assuming that it means put things on the blockchain/IPFS. And supposedly the purpose of this would be to make sure no single entity can withhold any scientific breakthroughs and it is available for public good. 

Okay let's say in vivo CRISPR technology is democratized so much so it is safe enough for n=1 trials. Maybe I feel like giving myself a 6th finger. It wants to make sure that data is recorded about a patient in a way that institutions cannot use it for profit, but rather for the public good. I like the sentiment here, but I am critical of its actual implementation. I feel like its more of a measurement problem. 1) How can I make sure collect consistent, relevant data with participants’ consent that decided to use in vivo CRISPR tech. Perhaps that is room for innovation? 2) make sure the culture and incentives are designed around so? Fundamentally, I am critical of that there are, in its current state, bottlenecks that decentralization solves, and why it outperform an openly accessible repository with well designed funding and reporting requirements? However, I am excited for a world where everyone is scientists and this is an actual problem.  

3) "Build network states with novel regulatory frameworks for safe, open clinical trials."
I sort of feel like moving on to this second principle, but I sort of addressed this in the last point. I feel like the main concern here is that nobody is able to use it for profit, or maybe so. I think that perhaps open-source GitHub repositories can provide a useful precedent for how to move forward. 

"2. ENGINEER ethical evolution
Biosafety and accountability can be built into the foundations of our technologies through smart contracts. These create immutable records that enable privacy but allow selective disclosure. Communities can define which gene sequences are considered pathogenic and enforce safety parameters. Smart contracts automate fail-safe measures and governance protocols, ensuring rapid response to risks. By leveraging encryption, onchain governance and consensus we create networks where innovation thrives within transparent, community-driven safety standards."
